body.iCan: I can assess the schoolyard environment.
successCriteria: I can assess the schoolyard using a checklist

body.hook: Before you can improve something, you need to know where it stands. Scientists and city planners start every project with an assessment. Today, your schoolyard is the study site.

vocabulary.definition: Collecting information to understand the current state of something.
The variety of living things in an area.

study.title: Schoolyard Check-Up
study.question: What is the state of our schoolyard environment?
study.passage:
Schoolyard assessment (written for this lesson):
Zones: divide the schoolyard into zones (front entrance, field, playground, parking edge, garden). Each group takes one.
1. Litter audit (with gloves and grabbers): collect litter in your zone for 15 minutes; sort into plastic, paper, food waste, metal, other; count and weigh. Never pick up sharp objects or needles: tell an adult.
2. Plant survey: count types of plants (grass, trees, shrubs, flowers, weeds); note any flowering plants for pollinators.
3. Habitat check: are there places for birds and insects (trees, shrubs, logs, water)? Evidence of animals?
4. Surfaces: estimate the percentage that is pavement vs grass vs garden vs bare soil.
5. Problems: drainage puddles, erosion, worn paths, areas with no shade.
Results: combine class data into a chart. This is your baseline. Vote on the biggest problem to solve (e.g. litter by the entrance, no pollinator plants, bare erosion patch).
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

body.objective: Students will be able to plan a stewardship action.
body.iCan: I can plan a stewardship action.
successCriteria: I can write a SMART goal for a stewardship action
I can plan tasks, materials, roles and a timeline
I can get permission and consider safety
body.hook: Good intentions aren't enough; projects need a plan. Who will do what, when, with which materials, and how will we know it worked? Today you plan a stewardship action for the schoolyard.

vocabulary.definition: Taking responsibility for caring for the environment.
A detailed plan of tasks, roles, materials and timeline.
A goal that is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
A plant that naturally grows in the region.
A schedule of when tasks will happen.
Approval from people responsible, such as the principal or facilities staff.

study.title: Planning Our Action
study.question: How do we plan a stewardship action that works?
study.passage:
Planning template (written for this lesson):
Project ideas (from the baseline): a regular litter patrol and new bin signs at the entrance; planting a pollinator patch with native Alberta plants (e.g. wild bergamot, prairie crocus, blanket flower, fireweed, goldenrod); building and installing bird or bee houses; mulching a bare erosion patch; a "no-idling" or waste-reduction campaign.
1. SMART goal: e.g. "By June 5, plant a 4 m² pollinator patch with at least 5 native species near the south fence."
2. Tasks: list each step in order.
3. Roles: project manager, materials coordinator, communications (posters, announcements), safety officer, data recorder.
4. Materials and budget: what you need, where it comes from (donations, school budget, local garden centres).
5. Timeline: dates for each task.
6. Permission: write a short proposal to the principal and facilities staff.
7. Safety: tools, gloves, weather, supervision.
8. Success measures: how will you compare with the baseline?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; native plant examples are common Alberta wildflowers.

body.objective: Students will be able to carry out and reflect on the action.

successCriteria: I can carry out my role in the stewardship action safely

body.hook: Action day. Gloves on, plan in hand. When the work is done, you'll measure the change, reflect on what you learned and share it, so others can do the same.

vocabulary.definition: Looking at before and after data to measure change.

study.title: Taking Action
study.question: How do we carry out, measure and share our stewardship action?
study.passage:
Action day and follow-up (written for this lesson):
1. Safety briefing (5 minutes): gloves, tools, boundaries, weather, buddies, what to do with sharp litter.
2. Action (40 minutes): carry out your roles. The data recorder takes photos (before, during, after) and notes.
3. Clean-up: return tools; leave the area tidy.
4. After-data (next week): repeat the baseline measurement (litter count, plant species, etc.) in the same zone and the same way.
5. Compare: make a before-and-after chart. Did you meet your SMART goal?
6. Reflect: What went well? What was hard? What would you change? How did it feel to make a difference?
7. Communicate: share through a morning announcement, newsletter blurb, poster or short presentation to another class.
8. Sustain: who will water the plants or continue the litter patrol? Write a care plan and hand it to a group or club.
